title: Notices filed after the twelve-month ban on donations had already run out
question: The notice is the public list of whose donations an approving official may not take for twelve months. How many notices arrived after those twelve months were over?
finding: 196 notices were filed more than 365 days after the approval they report, 186 of them from the Mayor’s office; they name 126 contractors and grantees, and 166 give the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development as the filer’s department. Most were signed in batches: 69 in 2023-05, 42 in 2024-10, 14 in 2022-12. The longest gap is 838 days (Homeless Prenatal Program, Inc, approved 2021-10-01, notice signed 2024-01-17). Across all notices, 2 donations ($500) by people named on a notice, who gave the contractor as their employer, went to a committee of the approving office after the approval and before the notice naming them was filed; 0 of those concern the contractors listed here.
how: A City agreement on disk states the period: the ban runs “until the later of either the termination of negotiations for such contract or twelve months after the date City approves the contract”. A notice filed more than 365 days after the approval date therefore reached the public list after the post-approval period it starts had ended. Rows are contractors with at least one such notice, by approving office; “over 90 days” counts that contractor’s other long-delayed notices too. The donation columns take the matches of the screen “Officers’ donations inside the contractor window” (the donor’s name is on the notice and the donor’s stated employer is the contractor) and keep those dated on or after the approval and before the day the notice was signed.
limits: A late notice does not make a donation improper or proper: the ban applies from the proposal whether or not the notice is on file, and the committee, not the contractor, files nothing here. What the delay removes is the public list that a campaign treasurer, a reporter or the Ethics Commission would check a donor against. The everyday reasons for the batches are a backlog cleared at once and yearly grant agreements. Donors are counted, never named; a name and employer match is strong but is not proof of identity.
